dietEvidence.body: The small fluted teeth and jaw apparatus are consistent with herbivory. No gut contents are known, and the plants eaten are not preserved.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: An ankylosaurid with a broad, low body, fused armour and a heavy tail club. The club is bone; its impact force is modelled, not observed.
summary: An ankylosaurid with a broad, low body, fused armour and a heavy tail club. The club is bone; its impact force is modelled, not observed.

discovery.body: First described as Stereocephalus tutus by Lawrence Lambe in 1902 from the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta. Because the genus name was preoccupied by a beetle, Lambe proposed Euoplocephalus in 1910. The holotype, CMN 0210, is a fragmentary skull roof, part of the first cervical half-ring and a rib.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Several skulls and partial skeletons, including articulated armour.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Dinosaur Park Formation, Alberta records the species in the Late Cretaceous. The numeric range used here is ≈77–75 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is broad and heavily fused, the body is covered in osteoderms, and the tail ends in a large bony club.

behaviour.body: Herbivory is inferred from the dentition and jaw apparatus. The tail club is usually interpreted as defensive, but no strike or predator interaction is preserved.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from several skulls and partial skeletons, including articulated armour. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The holotype is fragmentary, and most of the familiar postcranial anatomy comes from referred specimens. The old broad Euoplocephalus concept mixed several ankylosaurid taxa; the 2013 revision restricted the species. Soft-tissue referrals remain uncertain.
